title: Does a context switch always flush the TLB?

cast.name: Zed
cast.role: Repeats rules he read years ago

cast.name: Abi
cast.role: Kernel dev who reads the manual

glossary.note: A small cache of finished address translations.
An x86 tag on TLB entries, held in the low bits of CR3.
The arm64 tag on TLB entries.
Holds the arm64 page-table base and the ASID.

key_points: Without PCID, a CR3 write drops all non-global TLB entries.
With PCID or ASID tags, entries from different address spaces can coexist.
Setting bit 63 on the CR3 write tells x86 not to flush.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Zed repeats a rule he read years ago, as if it were physics.

visuals.text: claim: every context switch flushes the whole TLB

beats.speaker: zed
beats.text: Every context switch throws away the whole TLB. It has to.
beats.say: Every context switch throws away the whole T L B. It has to.

beats.speaker: abi
beats.text: The TLB caches translations, virtual page to frame. A hit is instant. A miss means a page walk.
beats.say: The T L B caches translations, virtual page to frame. A hit is instant. A miss means a page walk.

beats.speaker: abi
beats.text: Why ever flush? Two processes can use the same virtual page for different frames.

visuals.text: A, B use page 0x400: A in 0x91, B in 0x2c

beats.speaker: abi
beats.text: Untagged, B would hit A's entry: the wrong frame.

visuals.text: B hits A's entry: wrong frame

beats.speaker: abi
beats.text: So without PCID, loading CR3 on a switch drops every non-global entry, and the next accesses all miss.
beats.say: So without P C I D, loading C R three on a switch drops every non-global entry, and the next accesses all miss.

beats.speaker: zed
beats.text: Brutal. So the myth is right.

beats.speaker: abi
beats.text: Only on old settings. With PCID, the low twelve bits of CR3 tag each entry.
beats.say: Only on old settings. With P C I D, the low twelve bits of C R three tag each entry.

beats.speaker: abi
beats.text: Both entries coexist. Bit sixty-three set on the CR3 write says: don't flush.
beats.say: Both entries coexist. Bit sixty-three set on the C R three write says: don't flush.

beats.speaker: abi
beats.text: Arm64 tags entries with an ASID, held in the TTBR. Cleaning other cores differs: x86 sends interrupts, arm64 broadcasts TLB invalidate instructions.
beats.say: Arm sixty-four tags entries with an A S I D, held in the T T B R. Cleaning other cores differs: x eighty-six sends interrupts, arm sixty-four broadcasts T L B invalidate instructions.

visuals.sub: PCID tag, interrupts to other cores

beats.speaker: zed
beats.text: So a switch can be just a register write.

beats.speaker: abi
beats.text: Yes. A flush is a choice, not a law.
